Make no mistake, this is about prosecuting the press, and this isn’t the first time something like
this has happened to me.
In New Orleans, LA, they falsely accused me of a felony and later admitted there was no felony.
The U.S. attorneys involved in that case were eventually disbarred.
The federal prosecutor was so furious about this case that he literally threw my book at me.
“You’re a nasty, little, cowardly spud,” prosecutor Jim Letten said. “You are scum! I recused from
your case!”
Then there was the case when the FBI came knocking at my house. Agents stormed into my
home and unlocked my phone to get access to my Signal in order to intimidate me and to

It was such a landmark First Amendment case that the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU)

I went up to the 1st Circuit Court of Appeals in Massachusetts there. We won a partial victory.
In another civil case, Shirley Teter v. O’Keefe, I won at directed verdict. For that case, there were
six pro-bono lawyers representing the plaintiff, who stated, “We’re not paid by the Hillary
Clinton campaign or by the Democratic Party or anything like that.” The federal judge pointed
out the unsolicited statement only raised further questions, and ordered them to pay my legal
fees.
I have been sued so many times and have had so many criminal threats made against me that
even the media that hates me is forced to acknowledge that I have established legal 1st
Amendment precedent throughout the nation.
We also overturned a jury verdict against me in the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals last month

involved.

The politics of fear and weaponized lawfare don’t seem to work against me. It never has.

Why is that? It’s because what’s at issue here is not actually political; it’s fundamental.
This is about whether citizens still have a right to ask questions of their government servants,
and such a fundamental right will always prevail if you do not cower at their threats.
And the thing about me is – I never settle.
Most people find lawsuits stressful. The process becomes a form of punishment, but not to me.
I actually love this process.
I enjoy this process.
I'm going to have fun with this process.
Because it allows me to expose injustice at the highest levels.
There is nothing as sweet as justice, and there is nothing as motivating as injustice.
And in this case, they have put your right to speak on the line. Everything we believe in as
Americans has been put on the line.
But it does seem to indicate the direction of where our country is going.
I recognize that we’re well past the point of being completely divided in this country, but this

🔊 Iran foreign minister offers condolences to Spain over deadly train crash

📌 Tehran, IRNA – Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has conveyed condolences to Spain over a train crash that left dozens of people dead.

In a message sent on Friday to his Spanish counterpart Jose Manuel Albares, the Iranian foreign minister offered condolences on behalf of himself, the Iranian people and government over the fatal incident.
​
He said Iran was deeply saddened by the tragedy and asked Albares to accept his sincere sympathy.
​
The crash involved two passenger trains in central Spain, leaving at least 68 people dead and dozens injured. It occurred on Wednesday morning near Oreda station in Toledo province, about 140 kilometers south of Madrid.
​
Spain’s prime minister declared three days of national mourning and ordered an immediate investigation into the cause. Fifty-three injured people remained in hospital, while 56 others had been discharged.

Crypto Idea

AI could turn out to be both the greatest technological revolution of the past few decades and one of the biggest investment bubbles in history.

Yesterday, Anthropic reported a net loss of $80.7 billion in just the first half of the year. To be fair, there’s no need to panic over the headline number itself. Around $72 billion of that loss came from an accounting revaluation of the company’s liabilities, not from Anthropic actually burning through that much cash. But something else is far more interesting.

The company has already committed hundreds of billions of dollars to computing capacity, chips, and data centers. And Anthropic is far from alone. Amazon, Microsoft, Google, and Meta are set to invest more than $700 billion in AI infrastructure this year. The scale has become so enormous that these investments are now supporting the U.S. stock market and accounting for a significant share of investment activity across the economy.

And this is where the U.S. is gradually falling into a very interesting trap. If tech companies keep spending at this pace, they’ll have to borrow more and more money and somehow prove that these massive investments will actually pay off. If they start cutting spending, the fallout will hit chipmakers, data centers, the energy sector, the tech companies themselves, and ultimately the stock market.

In other words, the AI boom is becoming too big to simply bring to a halt without serious consequences. The IMF already estimates that a sharp pullback in AI investment could leave the U.S. economy around 1.8% smaller by 2028 than it would be under the current baseline scenario.

Anthropic’s IPO in November could become the first serious test of this whole setup. Not long ago, the market was discussing a valuation of around $2 trillion for the company. Following the latest figures, some investors are now talking about roughly $1.5 trillion. At the same time, the business itself continues to grow at an extraordinary pace.

From a capital markets perspective, I see the main risk here as something other than AI itself. I have little doubt that it will fundamentally reshape the economy and the world. But the gap between the hundreds of billions being invested today and the point at which those investments start generating comparable returns could be much longer than the market currently expects. That’s precisely where the risk of today’s euphoria lies. Major technological shifts almost never happen quickly or without friction.

Few moments sum up our complicated relationship with phones quite like this one.

At a U2 concert, the screen flashed: “Social media is the Antichrist.” A sharp reminder to keep things in perspective.

Kissing the lips you love, waking up in someone’s arms, drifting off with your head on their shoulder while watching a great film, and looking forward to every moment together—that’s happiness. Simple, everyday, human happiness, so easy to overlook when we’re chasing money, power, and all the rest.
